episode.title: Frame the Decision: Pragmatic Threat Models
episode.description: Threat modeling, secure defaults, secrets handling, supply chain risks, and what “shift left” should actually mean.

feed.description: Software engineering conversations: reliability, architecture, delivery, and the tradeoffs nobody puts in the blog post.
feed.title: Practical Systems

bullets: Threat modeling is a framing exercise — framing the decision wrong leads to building the wrong defenses, which is why the initial framing determines the quality of security outcomes.
Authn/authz separation matters more than people think, and this pattern holds across multiple teams, indicating it's a foundational element of secure design.
Security incidents are reliability incidents — a structural insight that reveals how failure modes in security often stem from operational and system reliability issues.
Compliance work like Vanta-style SOC 2 and ISO certification overlaps with real security work by only about 60%, meaning the bulk of security must be addressed operationally, not just procedurally.
The frame for a security review should be 'what could go wrong if this assumption is wrong' — this question drives better decisions and prevents redundant work down the line.
Tools like Sentry, Linear, and Datadog reveal failure modes more clearly when used in context — their presence amplifies visibility into system behavior and incident patterns.
When teams adopt PagerDuty in incident workflows, the trade-offs become visible — the tooling reveals the assumptions and priorities embedded in the process.
The most underrated piece of security design is not a tool or a checklist but a mindset: the ability to reframe risk as operational uncertainty and act accordingly.
